title: Puck Line Betting in Canada: An NHL Bettor's Guide
excerpt: How the NHL puck line really works, why empty-net goals wreck -1.5 tickets, and when +1.5 is the smarter price. A practical guide for Canadian bettors.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Puck line betting is the closest thing hockey has to a point spread, and it is the market most Canadian bettors reach for when a moneyline price looks too short to bother with. The concept is simple: instead of asking who wins, the puck line asks whether the favourite wins by two or more goals. Getting from that one-sentence definition to actually beating the market is a longer trip. Ahead of the 2026-27 season, here is how the puck line works, where the number lies to you, and when it is worth your money.

What the puck line is, and how it differs from the moneyline

A moneyline bet is a straight question. Team wins, you collect. Overtime and shootout results count, so a game decided in the eighth round of a skills competition pays exactly the same as a 6-1 romp.

The puck line takes that same game and applies a 1.5-goal handicap. The favourite is listed at -1.5 and must win by two or more. The underdog is listed at +1.5 and cashes if they win outright, lose in overtime or a shootout, or lose by exactly one goal in regulation. Because that handicap is meaningful in a sport where most games are decided by a single goal, the prices swing hard. A team that is -190 on the moneyline might be +155 at -1.5, while the other side flips from +160 to roughly -185.

That inversion is the entire appeal. Backing a heavy favourite at -1.5 turns a bad price into a plus-money one. Taking +1.5 on a live underdog turns a coin-flip payout into a high-probability, low-return ticket. Neither of those is automatically good. Both are just repriced versions of the same game.

Why hockey uses a fixed 1.5-goal spread

Football and basketball use variable spreads because scoring is granular enough to support them. Hockey is not. Final scores cluster tightly, and the difference between a mismatch and a pick'em is often less than a goal of true expectation. A sportsbook cannot offer a 0.5 or 2.5 hockey spread on most games without one side becoming absurd.

So the industry standardised on 1.5 and moved the price instead of the number. This is why puck line odds look so extreme compared to a football spread. All the information about team strength gets compressed into the juice rather than the handicap. If you are new to reading these markets, our guide to sports betting fundamentals covers how odds formats and payouts translate before you start comparing puck line prices across books.

The empty-net factor

Nothing distorts puck line results more than the empty net. Trailing teams pull the goalie earlier every season, often with three minutes or more remaining, sometimes on a delayed penalty far outside that window. The result is a wave of late scoring that has nothing to do with how the previous 57 minutes went.

The practical consequences are worth spelling out:

  • A one-goal game becomes a two-goal game after the buzzer beater into the empty cage, converting a losing -1.5 ticket into a winner and vice versa on +1.5.
  • Trailing teams also score with the extra attacker, which means the empty net cuts both ways and can rescue a +1.5 bet that looked dead.
  • Teams that protect leads well and have a strong penalty kill tend to be better empty-net closers than their goal differential suggests.
  • A favourite leading by two late is often insulated, because the trailing team will not pull the goalie as aggressively, which removes the cushion you were counting on.

Empty-net goals are a meaningful share of late third-period scoring in the modern NHL, and they are largely uncorrelated with the run of play. That is noise, not skill. If your entire edge on a -1.5 play depends on a late insurance marker, you do not have an edge. You have a coin flip with worse variance.

When to take -1.5 and when to take +1.5

The case for the favourite

Laying -1.5 makes sense when the favourite is genuinely dominant rather than merely better, and when the game script encourages a blowout. Look for a large goaltending gap, a rested team against the back end of a road back-to-back, a heavy shot-share mismatch, and an opponent that plays an open, high-event style. Teams that trail early and chase the game concede in bunches. That is where two-goal wins live.

The case for the underdog

Taking +1.5 is the better price when a competent underdog is priced up for reasons that have little to do with the on-ice matchup. Public-heavy favourites, marquee Original Six clubs and teams coming off a headline win all get shaded. If the underdog is defensively sound, gets solid goaltending and plays a low-event structure, +1.5 quietly wins a lot of games it has no business winning, because overtime and shootout losses still pay.

The honest answer is that neither side is systematically profitable. Books price the puck line carefully. Your edge comes from specific situations, line shopping and the discipline to pass, not from a rule of thumb.

Implied probability and finding the vig

Convert every price before you bet. For a plus-money line, implied probability is 100 divided by the odds plus 100. So +155 is 100 / 255, or about 39.2 per cent. For a minus line, it is the odds divided by the odds plus 100. So -185 is 185 / 285, or about 64.9 per cent.

Add both sides. If they total more than 100, the excess is the sportsbook's margin. Puck lines frequently carry a wider margin than moneylines on the same game, which is one of the quiet reasons this market is harder to beat than it looks. Comparing the same game across a few books is the single highest-value habit a Canadian bettor can build, and our DraftKings sportsbook review is a useful reference point for how one major operator prices its NHL board.

Alternate lines, 60-minute markets and three-way betting

The standard puck line is one option among several. Alternate lines let you move the handicap to -2.5 or +2.5 at a repriced number, which is useful when your read is about margin rather than outcome. A -2.5 play on a team facing an exhausted backup goaltender is a cleaner expression of that view than -1.5.

Sixty-minute and three-way markets remove overtime entirely. You bet home win, away win or draw in regulation. This matters enormously, because a large share of NHL games reach the third period tied or within a goal. A three-way home win is a materially different bet from a moneyline, and the draw is often the most underrated selection on the board. Just know which one you clicked. Confusing a three-way line with a puck line is the most common unforced error new hockey bettors make.

Puck line parlays and correlation

Stacking multiple -1.5 favourites into a parlay is a popular way to lose money quickly. Each leg is roughly a coin flip with vig attached. Four of them is not a value play, it is a lottery ticket priced like one.

Correlation is the part worth understanding. Legs within the same game can be linked: a -1.5 favourite and the over often move together, because blowouts are high-scoring. Most books account for this by restricting or repricing same-game combinations. Legs across different games are independent, so combining them multiplies the hold against you with no offsetting benefit. If you parlay, do it small and do it knowing the maths.

The Canadian picture and bankroll discipline

Single-game wagering has been legal across Canada since August 2021, but the shape of the market depends on where you live. Ontario has run a competitive regulated market with dozens of licensed operators since April 2022, and Alberta became the country's second open regulated market on 13 July 2026. Everywhere else, legal betting runs through the provincial lottery corporation, which typically means fewer alternate lines and less favourable pricing on hockey. Bettors can compare what is available in their region through our Ontario sports betting hub or the broader Canadian sports betting section.

Whatever province you are in, the discipline is identical. Set a unit size around one to two per cent of your bankroll and hold it steady. Do not raise stakes to recover a bad night. Track your bets by market type so you can see whether your puck line results are actually positive or just memorable. Hockey is a high-variance sport, and the 1.5-goal line adds another layer of randomness on top. Long losing stretches are normal even when your process is sound, which is exactly why the process has to come first.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
